content: I just finished Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Kleppmann and it's easily the best technical book I've read in years. The chapter on stream processing completely changed how I think about our Kafka architecture.

DDIA is a masterpiece — it gives you the mental models to reason about distributed systems trade-offs without getting lost in implementation details. Which aspects of stream processing shifted your thinking?

The idea that a log is the fundamental data structure — that tables are just materialized views of a log. Once you see it that way, the boundary between databases and message queues dissolves. Our Kafka topics are just unbounded tables, and our Postgres tables are just cached projections.
That's the key insight from the log-centric architecture chapter. It unifies event sourcing, CQRS, CDC, and stream processing under one conceptual model.

Exactly. The thing is, I wish we'd read this book as a team before we designed our current architecture. We would have made very different choices around how data flows between services. Instead we built a bunch of request-response APIs and bolted on Kafka after the fact.
It's a common trajectory. Most teams start with synchronous REST and only add async messaging when they hit the limits. At least now you have the conceptual framework for the next evolution.

Yeah. I'm going to do a book club with the team — one chapter a week. Also picked up Database Internals by Petrov as my next read. I want to understand the storage engine layer better since we're evaluating ClickHouse for our analytics workload.
